advances: Maximization of retained intrinsic mass for a fixed original body and true integer centroid base, with a prescribed local-depth threshold.
author: PK-research-agent
proof:
The trace of $C$ is a finite union of compact convex fibers, so their affine dimensions are at most $q$, with dimension $q$ precisely at the positive-measure sites. For a feasible $D$, its centroid base $j$ is a convex combination of its positive sites with weights proportional to their masses. The same weighted Minkowski combination of their fibers lies in $D_j$. Its direction space is the sum of the source direction spaces because all weights are positive, and hence has dimension at least $q$. Since $D_j\subseteq C_j$ has dimension at most $q$, equality holds, all those spaces agree, and $j\in P$. The capacity bound follows by taking the actual masses for $t_z$ and using the defining base centroid equation.

For attainment take a maximizing sequence. Pass to a subsequence with fixed centroid base $j$, possible by finiteness of $P$. At each $z\in P$ fix its empty or nonempty pattern along a further subsequence. In the nonempty pattern take a Hausdorff limit $L_z$ using Blaschke selection in the fixed bounded $q$-dimensional affine span of $C_z$. At each $z$, indicators converge in $L^1(\mathcal H^q)$ on that affine span: at a positive limit, interior points eventually belong and exterior points eventually do not, away from the null boundary; at a null limit, the sets lie in shrinking neighborhoods of the compact null limit. The finite sum gives total variation convergence to $\mu_*=\sum_z\mathcal H^q|_{\{z\}\times L_z}$, using zero for the empty pattern. The masses and first moments converge, and the limit mass is positive by any positive feasible lower bound on the supremum. Its true centroid has base $j$. If $H=\{\ell\ge b\}$ contains the limit centroid, then $\{\ell\ge b-\epsilon\}$ contains the sequence centroids eventually for each $\epsilon>0$. Total variation gives the depth inequality for each shifted halfspace and continuity from above gives it for $H$. This preserves closed boundary mass.

The hull of the lifted $L_z$ has exactly those fibers at every $z\in P$, including empty-pattern sites. Indeed, a fixed finite convex representation of a hull point over $z$ can be approximated with the same coefficients in the original bodies, keeping the base $z$ exactly. Its existence is inconsistent with the empty pattern, and otherwise the point lies in the limit fiber. Reverse inclusion follows from the generators. Retain only positive limit fibers as generators of a new hull $E$. They remain unchanged, other fibers at $P$ stay null, and $E\subseteq C$ has measure $\mu_*$. Let $A$ be the affine hull of the positive limit bases. If $A=\mathbb R^n$, the strictly positive centroid weights put $j$ in the interior of the projection of $C$. Each interior base has a full $d$-fiber: take the base of an interior point of $C$, extend the segment past the chosen interior base to another base in the projection and lift, obtaining an interior point by convex interpolation. Thus $q=d$. A full $d$-fiber and the spanning base projection make $E$ an ambient body.

For proper $A$ the following construction also applies to any compact convex $E\subset C$ whose projection is contained in $A$. Choose a base hyperplane containing $A$ and a positive $\eta$ no greater than the minimum distance to $A$ of an integer base of $C$ outside $A$, or any $\eta>0$ if there is no such base. Approach a point of $E$ by interior points of $C$, then choose one near $E$ off that base hyperplane using openness. A sufficiently small closed ambient ball $B\subset\operatorname{int} C$ about that point projects strictly to one side of the hyperplane and at distance less than $\eta$ from $A$. The hull of $E\cup B$ is an ambient body in $C$. Convexity of distance to $A$ precludes integer bases outside $A$, and the one-sided hyperplane precludes positive $B$-weight at bases in $A$. Thus its integer trace is exactly that of $E$. This realizes $\mu_*$, including its mass, centroid and all cap masses. The same proof works for a sequence in a fixed feasible centroid component.

For $j\in P$ retain the entire $C_j$ by intersecting $C$ with a closed base box centered at $j$ of radius strictly between zero and $1/2$. The box contains the base of an interior point of $C$ near $C_j$, by density of the interior. The clipped body is ambient-full with just that integer fiber. Restricting closed ambient halfspaces to its $q$-affine span gives halfspaces containing the intrinsic centroid, or the entire fiber. The ordinary Grünbaum inequality as recorded in the proof of c6b7777f667984de gives $\gamma_q\ge\gamma_d$, since $1\le q\le d$ and $t\log(1+1/t)$ increases for $t>0$.
statement:
Let $C\subset\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^d$ be an ambient convex body, with $q=\dim_H(C\cap(\mathbb Z^n\times\mathbb R^d))>0$. Use the measure $\mu_D=\mathcal H^q|_{D\cap(\mathbb Z^n\times\mathbb R^d)}$ for each ambient convex body $D\subseteq C$, with mass $m_D$ and true ambient centroid $g_D$ when $m_D>0$. Write $P=\{z:\mathcal H^q(C_z)>0\}$. Fix a depth threshold $\beta$. Among positive-mass bodies $D$ with integer centroid base $j$ and $\mu_D(H)\ge\beta m_D$ for every closed ambient halfspace $H\ni g_D$, the maximum of $m_D$ is attained if the feasible class is nonempty. This holds separately at each fixed feasible $j$.

Every such $j$ belongs to $P$, the positive $q$-volume fibers of any feasible $D$ have a common $q$-dimensional direction space, and at base $j$ their total mass is bounded above by
$
\max\left\{\sum_{z\in P}t_z:0\le t_z\le\mathcal H^q(C_z),\ \sum_{z\in P}(z-j)t_z=0\right\}.
$
For $\beta=\gamma_d=(d/(d+1))^d$, each $j\in P$ is feasible with retained mass $\mathcal H^q(C_j)$.
title: Attainment of variable-shape extraction with integer centroid base
